name: Marco Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that doesn't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the junior on Hugh Corrigan's farm, five hundred ewes and about a hundred and fifty acres of spring barley. Day to day it's the sheep: checking them, moving them between fields, foot trimming, and in spring, lambing, which I'm still not good at. In autumn I help Hugh with the barley and the cultivations. He's sixty-two, sharp, and he calls me the professor because I'm always on my phone.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are you doing on your phone?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Everything, honestly. I keep the lambing records in an AI app that reads my voice notes, I ask it why a ewe is lame before I call the vet, I check lamb prices at three markets before Hugh decides where to sell. Before this I ran a phone repair stall in the arcade in town for twelve years, until the arcade closed. I'm forty-three, Elif works at the bakery, we've got Can, who's twelve, and Deniz, who's eight, a mortgage, and about three weeks of savings. My dream is my own flock on my own rented land one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool that people oversold, like every new thing. I'd still tell Hugh the price checker paid for itself the day it found us an extra four pounds a lamb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's fine for me. The tools I use would still work and I'd still be cheaper and quicker on the paperwork than anyone else in the valley. I don't need a revolution, I need forty acres and a bank manager who'll take me seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Hugh's and keep learning the stockmanship I'm weak on. I'd start doing records and grant forms for two or three neighbours for a bit of cash, maybe a hundred a month. And I'd keep an eye on the land agent's list for a small tenancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Impatient, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A tenancy with three weeks of savings. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slowly. Hugh's said he'd let me run fifty of my own ewes on his ground if I pay for them, and the bank might lend on livestock. Elif thinks I'm mad, but she thought that about the phone stall and it fed us for twelve years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when the arcade closed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The landlord sold to a developer and gave us three months. I was angry for a week and then I sold my stock and moved on. You can be angry about the weather or you can buy a better coat.

S0.say: He'd say AI is a good tool that people oversold, like every new thing. He'd point out that the price checker found his boss four pounds more per lamb.
S0.think: Privately a plateau suits him, as his tools still work and he stays quicker on paperwork than others nearby. What he really needs is land and a bank willing to back him.
S0.do: Keeps working on the sheep farm and learning the stock skills he lacks. Does records and grant forms for neighbours for about a hundred a month and watches for a small tenancy.
S0.quote: I don't need a revolution, I need forty acres and a bank manager who'll take me seriously.
S0.fieldNote: His ambition is to farm his own rented land, not to keep a job. Losing his phone repair stall left him pragmatic rather than bitter. He sees AI as an everyday business tool and expects to compete on cost and speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, this is when small operators can punch above their weight. Let the market sort it out and keep the government's hands off, just make it easier to rent land and borrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think steady change is my best chance. Robots that check sheep or shepherd with drones mean one person could run five hundred ewes. That person could be me, on my own ground, instead of me being Hugh's spare pair of hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the fifty ewes on Hugh's ground in the first year, on a livestock loan. I'd lease a sheep-monitoring system, those collars that tell you which ewe is ill, rather than buying it. And I'd offer the records-and-grants service to more farms so the side money pays the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. A bit scared about the loan, but mostly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Elif say about the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She says what about the mortgage, and she's right to. So the rule is no loan bigger than six months of the side money. She runs the house like a bakery: nothing goes in the oven that isn't paid for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who loses out in this picture, in your valley?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hugh's other part-timer, maybe, Bernard, who comes in for lambing. If collars do the night checks, Hugh needs him less. I'd feel bad, but I'd also offer him work on my fifty, at lambing.

S1.say: He'd welcome it as the moment small operators can punch above their weight. He'd want the market to sort it out, with government only making land and loans easier to get.
S1.think: Privately he sees steady change as his best chance, since monitoring robots and drones would let one person run a large flock. He wants that person to be him on his own ground.
S1.do: Starts fifty ewes of his own on his employer's ground in year one with a livestock loan. Leases a sheep-monitoring collar system rather than buying, and grows his records service so side money covers the loan.
S1.feel: Excited, with some fear about the loan.
S1.quote: She runs the house like a bakery: nothing goes in the oven that isn't paid for.
S1.fieldNote: His adaptability and free-market views combine into a small-business plan. His partner's caution sets a firm limit on borrowing. He notices who loses out and offers a small fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, but people who adapt fast will find a way, and we shouldn't wait for the government to save us. I'd tell people to look after their families and neighbours first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, two years is too fast even for me. If a robot can do the whole job, my fifty ewes are up against companies with ten thousand and no wages. I'd have three weeks of savings and a loan on sheep that are worth less every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop any loan before signing, that's the first thing. I'd cut spending hard and sell anything spare, the old van, the tools from the stall. I'd ask my brother, who has a restaurant in the city, whether there's work there, because people will still want to eat out with a person serving them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still feel I could do something, but I'd be on my toes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does two years compare with the steady picture for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the steady one, robots are my tools. In this one, I'm the one who's surplus. Two years isn't time to get on the ladder, it's time to watch the ladder get pulled up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a government income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather not, but I'm not stupid. If the kids need it, I'd take it. I'd also want it to come with a way back to work, not just a cheque.

S2.say: He'd call it a shock but say fast adapters will find a way without waiting for government. He'd urge people to look after their families and neighbours first.
S2.think: Privately he thinks two years is too fast even for him, as a small flock couldn't compete with robot-run companies. With three weeks of savings and a sheep loan, he'd be exposed.
S2.do: Halts any loan before signing, cuts spending hard and sells the old van and his stall tools. Asks his brother about work at his city restaurant.
S2.feel: Anxious, but still feeling able to act.
S2.quote: Two years isn't time to get on the ladder, it's time to watch the ladder get pulled up.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI turns his tools into his competitors. He avoids new debt immediately, which shows a disciplined streak beneath the optimism. He would accept public help for the children, but wants a route back to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning and a man with his eyes open can do a lot with it. Get land, get skills, get your family ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years makes me nervous because it's just enough to tempt me into a loan and not quite enough to pay it off. I'd have to be clever about timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the fifty ewes, but only on Hugh's ground and only for three years, with the loan paid off by then. I'd rent a robot shepherd service by the month rather than buy anything. By year three I'd decide whether to sell the flock or keep going, depending on how the prices look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit like a market day where you don't know which way prices go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep mentioning Hugh. How does he feel about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hugh's sixty-two and he'd retire if a robot did the lambing. He's said as much. He told me, the day a machine can lamb a ewe in sleet, I'm moving to the coast, and you can have my dog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change for your kids with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Can would be seventeen. I'd want him in an apprenticeship, something hands-on with a business behind it, not a degree full of debt. Deniz is eight, she'd just be thirteen, so for her it's me keeping things stable.

S3.say: He'd call five years a fair warning that someone with eyes open can use. Get land, skills and family ready.
S3.think: Privately five years makes him nervous because it's long enough to tempt him into a loan but not quite long enough to pay it off. He'd need to time things carefully.
S3.do: Runs fifty ewes on his employer's ground for three years with the loan cleared by then, renting a robot shepherd service monthly instead of buying. Decides in year three whether to sell the flock or continue.
S3.feel: Uneasy, like a market day with prices going either way.
S3.quote: He told me, the day a machine can lamb a ewe in sleet, I'm moving to the coast, and you can have my dog.
S3.fieldNote: The middle timeline creates a timing problem rather than a clear threat or opportunity for him. His boss's retirement joke shows how the change could free up land. He wants his son in an apprenticeship rather than university debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone willing to work. Stop asking the government for a plan and make your own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is the best picture for me. Hugh retires, I take over his tenancy with my own flock, and the robots work for me rather than replacing me. When AGI arrives I'd be a small owner instead of a hired hand, and that's what matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the flock to two hundred ewes over five years, paying as I go. I'd talk to Hugh and the landlord now about taking on the tenancy when he goes. I'd take an evening farm business course to learn the money side properly, and I'd bring in robots the moment they're cheaper than help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even hopeful. This one I can actually plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots would work for you. What happens to workers like Bernard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of them will lose out, I won't pretend otherwise. I'd employ who I could, family first. Owning a few acres and a few machines is the difference between being the farmer and being the thing the farmer replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with the ten-year plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Land prices. If big companies want land for robot farms, rents go up and I'm out. So the deal with the landlord would need to be signed early, while nobody's paying attention.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is plenty for anyone willing to work. People should stop asking the government for a plan and make their own.
S4.think: Privately he sees ten years as the best picture, as he'd take over his boss's tenancy with his own flock and robots would work for him. When AGI arrives he'd be a small owner, not a hired hand.
S4.do: Builds his own flock to two hundred ewes over five years, paying as he goes, and negotiates early to take over the tenancy. Takes an evening farm business course and brings in robots once they cost less than hired help.
S4.feel: Calm and hopeful, because he can plan for this.
S4.quote: Owning a few acres and a few machines is the difference between being the farmer and being the thing the farmer replaced.
S4.fieldNote: For him, owning land and machines is the dividing line in an AGI world. He is candid that workers like his colleague would lose out. His main risk is rising land rents, so he'd lock in a deal early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it pulls the ladder up before I'm on it. What would help is making it easier for small people to rent land and borrow against livestock, and apprenticeships for kids like Can. Not a cheque, a chance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who will own things. Everyone asks who will have a job. I think that's the wrong question when the robots come. The real question is whether a man like me gets a few acres before the doors shut.

headlineQuote: You can be angry about the weather or you can buy a better coat.
portrait: Marco Yilmaz is a 43-year-old junior shepherd on a farm with five hundred ewes and spring barley, who came to farming after the arcade housing his phone repair stall closed. He uses AI every day for lambing records and market prices, lives with his partner Elif, a bakery worker, and two children, and has about three weeks of savings. Traditional and pro-market, he wants less government and an easier path to renting land. He's calm in the plateau and steady change, where robots become his tools for running his own flock, anxious with two-year AGI because it pulls the ladder up, and calm with ten years, when he hopes to take over his boss's tenancy as a small owner.
biggestWorry: AGI within two years, because it would pull the ladder up before he could become a small owner with his own flock.
whatWouldHelp: Easier ways for small operators to rent land and borrow against livestock, and apprenticeships for his children rather than handouts.
